The same central guarantee for both algorithms appears in PDF 1 abstract, PDF 2 contribution 2 and PDF 19 conclusion. The forced actions are Algorithm 1 (PDF 10) and Algorithm 2 (PDF 12).

Claim.

Under Assumptions 1–4, the graph-only LP value \(\sum_jz_j^*\) is \(\Theta(c_\mu)\), and the two proposed policies attain the \(c_\mu\log T\) regret lower bound within a multiplicative factor independent of network structure and time. Assumption 4 requires only that the number of optimal actions, the minimum suboptimal reward gap, and \(\min_iJ_i\) are constants independent of network sizes \(N,K\). Equation (2) itself contains \(\max_iJ_i\) and an additive number of optimal actions; neither is controlled as needed for the subsequent inference.

Error and reproducible evidence.

The following family satisfies every printed assumption, has a strictly positive lower-bound coefficient bounded as the network grows, and makes both actual policies incur a logarithmic coefficient growing linearly in network size. All suboptimal action means and gaps are exactly fixed across the family.

For each \(N\ge3\), let independent base variables be \(X_i=2Y_i+Z_i\), where \(Y_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(3/4)\), \(Z_i\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\theta_i)\), independently over variables and time. The univariate four-atom density is

\[ g_\theta=( (1-\theta)/4,\ \theta/4,\ 3(1-\theta)/4,\ 3\theta/4),\qquad \theta\in(0,1). \]

Its mean is \(u(\theta)=3/2+\theta\), and its KL divergence is exactly the Bernoulli KL \(D_B(\theta\Vert\sigma)\). Finiteness, continuity and denseness(Assumptions 1–3) hold. Discrete densities are permitted, as in the paper's Bernoulli examples.

There are \(K=N+1\) actions, indexed 0 through N. Action 0 observes base 1 and receives \(Y_1=\lfloor X_1/2\rfloor\). Action 1 observes base 1 and receives \(Z_1=X_1\bmod2\). Action 2 observes base 2 and receives \(Z_2\). For every \(i\ge3\), action i observes only base i and receives \(a_NZ_i\), where

\[ \delta_N=2^{-N^2},\qquad a_N=3/4+\delta_N. \]

Every reward-parent set is nonempty and equals its observed set; their union contains all base arms. All rewards are stochastic and in[0,1]. Choose \(\theta_1=\theta_2=1/2\) and \(\theta_i=1/(2a_N)=2/(3+4\delta_N)\) for \(i\ge3\). These true parameters remain inside[1/2,2/3]. Action 0 has mean 3/4 and is uniquely optimal; every other action has mean 1/2 and gap 1/4. The known Y marginal is allowed by the stated general bounded reward model; it is not an unknown parameter supplied to a policy.

For bases 1 and 2, the alternative parameter set is \((3/4,1)\), giving

\[ J_0=D_B(1/2\Vert3/4)=\tfrac12\log(4/3)>0. \]

Changing base 1's parameter leaves the optimal action's Y reward distribution unchanged. For every base i\(\ge3\), the alternative set is \((q_N,1)\), where \(q_N=3/(3+4\delta_N)\), giving

\[ J_N=\frac{2\log(2/3)+(1+4\delta_N)\log((1+4\delta_N)/(4\delta_N))}{3+4\delta_N} \sim\frac{N^2\log2}{3}. \]

\[ c_\mu=\frac{1}{4J_0}+\frac{N-2}{4J_N}\longrightarrow\frac{1}{4J_0}>0. \]

\[ \liminf_{T\to\infty}\frac{R_{\epsilon\text{-LP}}(T)}{\log T}\ge\frac{c}{d^2}\frac{N-1}{4}=256(N-1). \]

findings.title: Ambient Gaussian noise invalidates the claimed latent-dimension sample bound and its subspace recovery application
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v18-16-483__I01 — Ambient Gaussian noise invalidates the claimed latent-dimension sample bound and its subspace recovery application
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF page 59, Appendix G.5, Theorem 37 and its proof; PDF page 14, Section 3.5, the subspace sample-complexity comparison. The relevant model is specified on PDF page 12, Section 3.4; the affected estimator is Algorithm 3 on PDF page 13.

**Claim.** The subspace model draws
\[
x=U_iU_i^\top y+\xi,\qquad
y\sim N(0,I_d),\quad \xi\sim N(0,\sigma^2 I_d),
\]
where each \(U_i\) has \(m\) orthonormal columns. Theorem 37 sets
\[
\widehat A=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n x_jx_j^\top-\sigma^2I_d
\]
and asserts, together with a corresponding bound for \(\widehat B\), that
\[
\|\widehat A-A\|\le\epsilon
\]
with probability at least \(1-\delta\) when
\[
n\ge\widetilde\Omega\!\left(
\epsilon^{-2}(1+\sigma^2)\|v\|^2m\log(d/\delta)
\right).
\]
Section 3.5 explicitly presents the resulting \(m\)-scale sample bound as comparable to a noiseless subspace-clustering method while emphasizing that this method handles noisy samples. The noise covariance is \(I_d\), without a \(1/d\) normalization.

**Error and evidence.** Fix admissible parameters
\[
k=2,\quad m=1,\quad \alpha_1=\alpha_2=\tfrac12,\quad
U_1=e_1,\quad U_2=e_2,\quad \sigma^2=1,\quad v=e_1.
\]
The subspaces are orthogonal and jointly independent, \(A=\tfrac12(e_1e_1^\top+e_2e_2^\top)\) has rank \(km=2\), and the unit side vector satisfies the stated affinity condition with any fixed margin in \((0,1/3)\).

Let \(X=[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\). Whenever \(n<d-2\), the span of the samples and \(e_1,e_2\) has dimension at most \(n+2<d\). Choose a unit vector \(u\) orthogonal to that span. Then
\[
Au=0,\qquad
\widehat Au=(XX^\top/n-I_d)u=-u,
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{\|\widehat A-A\|\ge1}
\]
for **every sample outcome**. In particular, for \(\epsilon=1/2\) the asserted event has probability zero, even when the noise variance is known exactly.

With all the displayed model parameters fixed, a sample size bounded by any fixed power of \(\log d\) is eventually below \(d-2\). Thus no dimension-independent hidden constant or fixed logarithmic factor in the stated sufficient rate resolves the contradiction. An ambient-dimension sample requirement is necessary for this estimator.

The failure also reaches the actual recovery algorithm, rather than only an intermediate covariance bound. Write \(D=d-2\), and let \(X_\perp\) be rows 3 through \(d\) of \(X\). These entries are independent standard Gaussians. For \(G=X_\perp^\top X_\perp\),
\[
\mathbb E\|G-DI_n\|_F^2=D(n^2+n).
\]
Markov's inequality gives
\[
\Pr\{\lambda_{\min}(G)<D/2\}
\le \frac{4(n^2+n)}D.
\]
On the complementary event, if \(D>4n\), every sample-span eigenvalue of \(\widehat A\) exceeds 1, whereas its singular values off that span equal 1. Hence Algorithm 3's leading \(km=2\) singular vectors lie in \(\operatorname{span}(X)\). Its unwhitening and final eigenspace remain in that span, for any input \(B\), including exact population \(B\).

On this event,
\[
\|P_{\operatorname{span}(X)}e_1\|^2
\le \frac{2\|X^\top e_1\|^2}{D}.
\]
Since \(\mathbb E\|X^\top e_1\|^2=3n/2\), including the exceptional event yields
\[
\mathbb E\|P_{\operatorname{span}(X)}e_1\|^2
\le\frac{4n^2+7n}{D}.
\]
For \(n=\operatorname{polylog}(d)\), this tends to zero. Consequently any defined unit rank-one output of Algorithm 3 has projector error against \(e_1e_1^\top\) tending to 1 in probability. The promised finite-sample application can therefore fail even with ideal side information.

The proof's specific error is its statement on page 59 that \(x/\sigma\) is an \(m\)-dimensional Gaussian vector. Under the stated ambient isotropic noise model, its covariance has full rank \(d\).

**Why it matters.** Noisy moment-based subspace search with near-\(m\), rather than ambient-\(d\), sample complexity is an expressly new application and statistical guarantee of the paper. That guarantee is false, and the specified algorithm can have asymptotically maximal subspace error at the promised rate. Repair requires dimension-dependent samples or materially different noise/information assumptions; a constant change or local moment-formula correction does not preserve the claimed result. This withdraws a principal advertised application-specific guarantee and calls for revision of the affected claim.

The conditional perturbation result in Theorem 6 and the other three model families are not refuted here. Nor is this a claim that every possible estimator fails when given \(v=e_1\), or that the reported finite-dimensional empirical comparisons are false.

**Discovery method.** Traced the subspace sample-complexity proof and noticed that it treated a sample with full ambient Gaussian noise as \(m\)-dimensional.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original full-size rendered model, Algorithm 3, comparison and Theorem 37; constructed the exact nullspace witness satisfying all assumptions; derived the Gaussian Gram second-moment/sample-span consequence; executed independent Algorithm 3 checks. A second reviewer independently rederived both proofs and ran separate controls.

The reproducible helper is an unpublished audit file; evidence and independent QA are in unpublished audit files. The 24 seeded algorithm checks corroborate the proof: for example, at \(d=16384,n=32\), one run has covariance witness norm 1 and projector error approximately 0.99999766. These are independent implementations, not claimed historical experiment reruns.

**Confidence.** High. The covariance contradiction is deterministic for every sample outcome; the algorithm consequence follows from explicit moment inequalities. Both were independently checked against the original assumptions. The finding does not depend on unavailable source code, unknown constants, simulation alone, or attribution of a historical empirical failure.

findings.title: The finite-iteration guarantee is proved for an optimizer that the ECM algorithm does not compute, using a false concavity step
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v18-17-019__I01 — The finite-iteration guarantee is proved for an optimizer that the ECM algorithm does not compute, using a false concavity step
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages8–9, Lemmas2–3 and Table1; pages13–15, Theorem13 and Corollary18; AppendixB pages29–32, Equations34–35 and Lemma24; embedded online supplement S.VI pages53–55, especially page54's bounding of termII. Page numbers refer to the original58-page PDF, including its embedded supplement.

**Claim.** The abstract on PDF1 and the main contribution on PDF3 explicitly promise a bound for the output directly from their fast high-dimensional ECM algorithm. Theorem13 explicitly applies to “our SCAN algorithm in Table1.” With Conditions6/8/10, initialization within a constant-radius ball about the true mixture parameter, the stated tuning schedule and sample size, it gives a finite-iteration Euclidean estimation-error bound consisting of a geometric optimization term plus a statistical floor. Corollary18 specializes this to sparse mean/precision estimation and supplies a stopping guideline. Table1 is an expectation/conditional-maximization algorithm: after one E-step it updates means and precisions conditionally. The paper emphasizes that the bound is for its fast ECM algorithm, whose penalty prevents an explicit joint update.

**Error and evidence.** The proof changes this output into a joint global optimizer. Equation35 on PDF29 states

\[
\Theta^{(t)}=\arg\max_{\Theta'}\{Q_n(\Theta'\mid\Theta^{(t-1)})-\lambda_n^{(t)}P(\Theta')\}.
\]

This supplies the essential basic inequality \(f(\widehat\Delta)\ge0\) in34. A conditional sweep does not have this property. This is distinct from correcting local update typos: even an exact, genuine conditional sweep need not be jointly stationary.

For a reproducible example, let \(p=1,K=2\), use observations \(1,3\), and take identical fitted components and weights \(1/2\). The E-step responsibilities are genuinely \(1/2\). For each component the variable part of the conditional objective is

\[
q(\mu,\omega)=\tfrac14\log\omega
-\tfrac14\omega\{1+(2-\mu)^2\}-.05|\mu|.
\]

Starting with \(\omega=.1\), its exact mean-block maximizer is \(\mu=1\): the positive-mean derivative equation is \(\tfrac12(.1)(2-\mu)=.05\). Its subsequent exact precision-block maximizer is \(\omega=1/[1+(2-1)^2]=.5\). At the resulting pair the mean derivative of the smooth part is \(.5(.5)(2-1)=.25\), while the positive-mean penalty derivative is only \(.05\). The final mean KKT residual is therefore \(.20\ne0\). Increasing this final mean by \(.01\), holding its precision fixed, increases the penalized conditional objective by exactly \(159/80000>0\). Both precisions are positive; both conditional blocks were solved exactly. Thus even a repaired true ECM sweep is not Equation35's joint optimizer. This example isolates the invalid optimizer substitution; it is not presented as a counterexample to Theorem13's conclusion satisfying every one of its separation and sample-size hypotheses.

The proof also contains an independently false step, so simply redefining the output to be the joint optimizer does not validate it. Lemma24 asserts a joint supporting-hyperplane inequality along the line from the estimate to the truth. Its proof treats separate concavity in mean and precision as sufficient. On PDF54, termII's actual precision gradient at \((\mu^{(2)},\Omega^{(2)})\) is replaced by the derivative of \(g(\Omega)\) defined while holding \(\mu^{(1)}\) fixed. The missing mean/precision cross term prevents that equality.

Here is an explicit violation even with a genuine joint global penalized maximizer. For scalar data \(-1,+1\), put

\[
Q(\mu,\omega)=\tfrac12\log\omega-\tfrac12\omega(1+\mu^2).
\]

For every positive mean-L1 penalty the joint global maximizer is \(\widehat\theta=(0,1)\). Take \(\theta^*=(4,1/10)\) and its midpoint with the maximizer, \(z=(2,11/20)\). Then

\[
Q(\theta^*)-Q(z)-\nabla Q(z)^\top(\theta^*-z)
=\frac{221}{110}+\frac12\log\frac2{11}
=1.156716862971696\ldots>0,
\]

opposite to Lemma24's asserted nonpositive value. This is not a precision-boundary or numerical-rounding effect. The inequality is strict and persists on an open neighborhood of the sample, which has positive probability under nondegenerate Gaussian sampling. An identifiable two-component extension uses distinct true means4 and5 with true precisions.1, identical conditioning components \((0,1)\), equal mixing weights and the same sample. The genuine responsibilities remain.5, the penalized joint maximizers remain \((0,1)\) in both components, and the half-weighted sum of the two supporting-hyperplane remainders is \(1.606716862971696\ldots>0\). Again, this refutes the printed auxiliary inequality and its proposed justification; it does not assert that all of Theorem13's assumptions hold in this fixture.

The abstract on PDF1 and the main contribution on PDF3 explicitly promise a bound for the output directly from their fast high-dimensional ECM algorithm. The proof changes this output into a joint global optimizer. Equation35 on PDF29 states

findings.title: The nonlinear multiplier bootstrap has the wrong null distribution
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v18-17-145__I01 — The nonlinear multiplier bootstrap has the wrong null distribution
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pages 10–11, Section 3.2, equations (17)–(21); page 14, Theorem 3, equation (29). The invalid approximation is in Appendix G.1, Lemma 20, pages 51–52, and Appendix G.3, Lemma 24, pages 58–59. Appendix B.2, page 31, explicitly uses Lemma 20 for Theorem 3. The same lemma supports the uniform-test proof in Appendix F; the counterexample below directly disproves Theorem 3, rather than asserting a separate counterexample to Theorem 4.

**Claim.** The paper draws independent standard normal multipliers \(\xi_i\), defines
\[
 \widehat\tau^B_{jk}(z)=
 \frac{\sum_{i\ne l}w_iw_l\,s_{il}(\xi_i+\xi_l)}
      {\sum_{i\ne l}w_iw_l(\xi_i+\xi_l)},\qquad
 \widehat\Sigma^B_{jk}(z)=\sin\{\pi\widehat\tau^B_{jk}(z)/2\},
\]
where \(w_i=K_h(Z_i-z)\) and
\(s_{il}=\operatorname{sign}(X_{ij}-X_{lj})\operatorname{sign}(X_{ik}-X_{lk})\).
It then multiplies the resulting score by the multiplier kernel denominator to obtain \(S^B\), and uses its conditional quantile to calibrate the supergraph test. Theorem 3 claims
\[
 \sup_{\alpha\in(0,1)}
 \left|\Pr_{H_0}\{\psi_{z_0|G}(\alpha)=1\}-\alpha\right|
 =O(n^{-c})
\]
under its stated smoothness, sparsity, variance and rate conditions.

The asserted reason for multiplying back the denominator is that the leading bootstrap term becomes Gaussian. This fails because the denominator in (17) is centered near zero, and the sine is applied **before** multiplication back.

**Error and evidence.**

Consider the following null model:

- \(d=2\), \(Z\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)\), and \(X\sim N(0,I_2)\), independently of \(Z\).
- The monotone transforms are the identity, and \(\Sigma(z)=\Omega(z)=I_2\) for all \(z\). The true graph and the specified supergraph are empty.
- \(z_0=1/2\), \(K(u)=\frac12\mathbf1_{\{|u|<1\}}\), and \(h=n^{-2/9}\). This kernel is expressly permitted in Assumption 4.3.
- Use the fixed estimator \(\widehat\Omega(z)=I_2\). The theorem expressly permits any estimator satisfying Assumption 4.4; this is a fixed function, not an oracle using an unknown parameter.

All relevant assumptions hold. Choose \(s=1,M=1,\rho=2\). The density and correlation functions are smooth and bounded as required. Here \(r_{2n}=0\), and \(r_{1n},r_{3n}=C\sqrt{\log n/(nh)}\) suffice uniformly in \(z\): condition on the \(Z_i\), apply bounded Kendall U-statistic concentration within each kernel window, and union-bound the at most \(n^2\) possible interval subsets. With probability tending to one their counts are at least \(cnh\), including boundary windows. Constant correlation creates no boundary bias. The nondegenerate variance is \(\pi^2/18\).

The bandwidth lies strictly in the proof's \(n^{-\nu}\), \(1/5<\nu<1/4\), regime. In particular,
\[
 \sqrt{nh}\,h^2=n^{-1/18},\quad
 \frac{\log n}{\sqrt{nh}}=n^{-7/18}\log n,\quad
 \frac1{nh^2}=n^{-5/9},\quad
 \frac{\log^7 n}{nh}=n^{-7/9}\log^7 n.
\]
Thus Theorems 1 and 3's conditions hold at polynomial rates.

Use the ordinary U-statistic definition explicitly given on PDF pages 5 and 70:
\[
 U_n[H]=\{n(n-1)\}^{-1}\sum_{i\ne l}H(Y_i,Y_l).
\]
The page-7 exposition has a separate normalization inconsistency. Equation (20) also has an extra factor two relative to this definition. The argument first grants correction of that factor; it then checks the literal factor separately.

Define
\[
 D_n=\sqrt{nh}\,U_n[w_iw_l(\xi_i+\xi_l)],\qquad
 N_n=\sqrt{nh}\,U_n[w_iw_l s_{il}(\xi_i+\xi_l)].
\]
Given the observations, these are exactly jointly Gaussian. Let \(m\) be the number of observations in the window. Then \(m/(2nh)\to1\). Kendall row means converge to
\[
 q(X_i)=(2\Phi(X_{i1})-1)(2\Phi(X_{i2})-1),\quad
 E q=0,\quad E q^2=1/9.
\]
Consequently their conditional covariance converges in probability to
\[
 \operatorname{Cov}_\xi(D_n,N_n)\longrightarrow
 \begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&2/9\end{pmatrix}.
\]
For example, with \(c_n=2(2h)^{-2}\sqrt{nh}/\{n(n-1)\}\), the coefficients of \(\xi_i\) are \(c_n(m-1)\) for \(D_n\) and \(c_n\sum_{l\ne i}s_{il}\) for \(N_n\). These give the displayed covariance directly.

The ordinary Kendall Hoeffding CLT gives the true one-edge signed statistic
\[
 S_n\Rightarrow S\sim N(0,\sigma^2),\qquad
 \sigma=\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt2}.
\]
The one-edge maximum in (16) is signed; duplicate off-diagonal orientations give the same value. No absolute-value modification is assumed here.

After granting the factor-two correction, the actual bootstrap instead converges conditionally to
\[
 B=\sqrt2\,U\,\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi V}{6U}\right),
 \qquad U,V\ \text{independent }N(0,1).
\]
The literal equation (20) gives \(2B\). The ratio \(N_n/D_n\) remains of constant order, with a Cauchy-type limit. It does not concentrate near the true Kendall correlation zero, so the sine cannot be linearized with a vanishing remainder.

This difference yields **actual quantile errors**, as follows. Write \(Q=1-\Phi\). Since
\[
 |B|\le\min\{\sqrt2|U|,\sigma|V|\}
\]
and \(B\) has a symmetric continuous distribution,
\[
 \Pr(B>1)\le 2Q(1/\sqrt2)Q(1/\sigma)
 =0.0424031155<0.05.
\]
The corrected bootstrap's 95th percentile is therefore below 1. But
\[
 \Pr(S>1)=Q(1/\sigma)=0.0884319181.
\]
The corrected procedure's asymptotic rejection probability at nominal 5% is therefore **greater than 8.8%**. This is not a small-sample or simulation error.

The literal normalization also fails the exact-size theorem. On the event
\[
 1\le |U|\le2,\qquad 1.7\le V\le2,
\]
the magnitude of the sine argument is at most \(\pi/3\). Using
\(\sin t\ge3\sqrt3\,t/(2\pi)\) for \(0\le t\le\pi/3\), we obtain
\[
 B\ge \frac{\sqrt6 V}{4}\ge\frac{17\sqrt6}{40}>1.
\]
That event has probability
\[
 2\{\Phi(2)-\Phi(1)\}\{\Phi(2)-\Phi(1.7)\}
 =0.0059296304>0.005.
\]
Hence the literal bootstrap's 99.5th percentile is greater than 2, while
\[
 \Pr(S>2)=Q(6\sqrt2/\pi)=0.0034570975<0.005.
\]
Its size also stays away from the asserted nominal level. Conservatism contradicts Theorem 3's stated absolute error guarantee.

For reproducibility, an additional one-dimensional calculation gives
\[
 \Pr(B>q)=\frac1\pi\int_0^\infty
 \frac{\exp[-q^2(1+r^2)/\{4\sin^2(\pi r/6)\}]}{1+r^2}\,dr.
\]
It yields \(q_{.95}(B)=0.8890353337\), \(q_{.95}(2B)=1.7780706674\), and respective actual null rejection probabilities **0.1149494118** and **0.0081698292**, instead of 0.05. The analytic inequalities above suffice independently of this quadrature.

The erroneous proof step is especially explicit in Lemma 24. With at least two observations in the window, \(U_n[\omega^B]\) is a centered Gaussian conditional on the observations, so it is nonpositive with probability \(1/2\). It cannot concentrate around \(f_Z^2=1\), as claimed on page 58. The first display on page 59 subtracts this deterministic 1 from a homogeneous multiplier sum and incorrectly identifies the result as a centered Gaussian sum. Equation (114), page 52, then uses the nonexistent concentration to bound the bootstrap denominator away from zero and control the sine remainder.

**Why it matters.** Calibrated supergraph and uniform edge inference are central advertised contributions, rather than an auxiliary lemma: the introduction explicitly identifies the new multiplier-bootstrap procedure as necessary for the second major inference contribution. The published procedure has the wrong null distribution even for two independent Gaussian variables with every theorem condition satisfied. Correcting its normalization does not restore nominal testing. Theorem 3 is false, and the shared bootstrap approximation supporting the uniform-test validity proof is invalid.

A valid replacement can bootstrap a centered estimated linear influence process, or introduce a perturbation near the fitted correlation together with appropriate centering. Those replace the central nonlinear centered-ratio resampling statistic and require revised definitions and validity arguments. They do not preserve the procedure whose validity is established as written. The ordinary single-edge Gaussian test and graph-estimation results can survive; their survival does not validate the main new bootstrap-based inference contribution. 

**Discovery method.** While tracing the nonlinear bootstrap proof, noticed that both numerator and denominator use mean-zero Gaussian multipliers, yet Lemma 24 treats the denominator as concentrating around a positive density value.

**Verification method.** Read all original pages and appendices; inspected the rendered equations and theorem statements; constructed the admissible Gaussian null; derived its true and conditional bootstrap limits and exact quantile inequalities; checked the limits by quadrature, two million independent Gaussian draws, and conditional original pair-sum calculations for \(n=1000,4000,16000\). An independent auditor rederived the covariance, bandwidth exponents and analytic rejection inequalities from the original PDF and agreed with the assessment of the finding's significance.

The authors' authentic January 2016 repository also implements the centered-ratio/sine procedure with ordinary U normalization. Twenty-five unmodified native R fixtures match the direct formula to \(1.36\times10^{-15}\). This corroborates the structural procedure; it does not establish the code used for the final 2018 tables. No historical table values or separate uniform-process counterexample are claimed.

**Confidence: High.** The failure follows from an exact admissible-null limit and explicit normal-probability inequalities, with independent mathematical QA. Numerical and native-code checks corroborate the derivation. The finding does not depend on interpreting missing artifacts or on attributing a particular implementation to the final empirical tables.

It yields \(q_{.95}(B)=0.8890353337\), \(q_{.95}(2B)=1.7780706674\), and respective actual null rejection probabilities 0.1149494118 and 0.0081698292, instead of 0.05. The analytic inequalities above suffice independently of this quadrature.

The erroneous proof step is especially explicit in Lemma 24. With at least two observations in the window, \(U_n[\omega^B]\) is a centered Gaussian conditional on the observations, so it is nonpositive with probability \(1/2\). It cannot concentrate around \(f_Z^2=1\), as claimed on page 58. The first display on page 59 subtracts this deterministic 1 from a homogeneous multiplier sum and incorrectly identifies the result as a centered Gaussian sum. Equation (114), page 52, then uses the nonexistent concentration to bound the bootstrap denominator away from zero and control the sine remainder.

Why it matters.

Calibrated supergraph and uniform edge inference are central advertised contributions, rather than an auxiliary lemma: the introduction explicitly identifies the new multiplier-bootstrap procedure as necessary for the second major inference contribution. The published procedure has the wrong null distribution even for two independent Gaussian variables with every theorem condition satisfied. Correcting its normalization does not restore nominal testing. Theorem 3 is false, and the shared bootstrap approximation supporting the uniform-test validity proof is invalid.

A valid replacement can bootstrap a centered estimated linear influence process, or introduce a perturbation near the fitted correlation together with appropriate centering. Those replace the central nonlinear centered-ratio resampling statistic and require revised definitions and validity arguments. They do not preserve the procedure whose validity is established as written. The ordinary single-edge Gaussian test and graph-estimation results can survive; their survival does not validate the main new bootstrap-based inference contribution.

Discovery method.

While tracing the nonlinear bootstrap proof, noticed that both numerator and denominator use mean-zero Gaussian multipliers, yet Lemma 24 treats the denominator as concentrating around a positive density value.

Verification method.

Read all original pages and appendices; inspected the rendered equations and theorem statements; constructed the admissible Gaussian null; derived its true and conditional bootstrap limits and exact quantile inequalities; checked the limits by quadrature, two million independent Gaussian draws, and conditional original pair-sum calculations for \(n=1000,4000,16000\). An independent auditor rederived the covariance, bandwidth exponents and analytic rejection inequalities from the original PDF and agreed with the assessment of the finding's significance.

The authors' authentic January 2016 repository also implements the centered-ratio/sine procedure with ordinary U normalization. Twenty-five unmodified native R fixtures match the direct formula to \(1.36\times10^{-15}\). This corroborates the structural procedure; it does not establish the code used for the final 2018 tables. No historical table values or separate uniform-process counterexample are claimed.

Confidence: High.

The failure follows from an exact admissible-null limit and explicit normal-probability inequalities, with independent mathematical QA. Numerical and native-code checks corroborate the derivation. The finding does not depend on interpreting missing artifacts or on attributing a particular implementation to the final empirical tables.

findings.title: The main coefficient error bound permits inconsistent estimators
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v18-17-159-01 The main coefficient error bound permits inconsistent estimators
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** Theorem4, PDFpage8; assumption(A5), PDFpage7; population target/Hessian, PDFpage6; dependent Taylor lower bound in AppendixA, PDFpage23. Page numbers count from the first PDF page.

**Claim.** Under(A1)–(A7), Theorem4 bounds the coefficient error by

sqrt(1+1/cbar) [2lambda sqrt(q)/M2 + (2C4/M2) q² sqrt((logp)³/n) (5/4+1/cbar)],

with probability at least1−3p^{−q(C2²−2)+1}. With the prescribedlambda, the paper concludes ||betahat−beta*||2=O_P(q²sqrt((logp)³/n)). The targetbeta* is the minimizer of its population weighted hinge riskL(beta), not an externally specified regression coefficient. Assumption(A5) only lowerbounds dᵀH(beta*)d/||d||² for directions that are BOTH q-sparse and in the statedl1cone. AppendixA applies that lower bound to h=beta*−betahat without establishing thath isq-sparse.

**Error and evidence.** The theorem is false under its written assumptions. The following continuous, bounded, iid model has fixed regularity constants, q1 andp>n, but every empirical minimizer has coefficient error bounded away fromzero with probability tending toone.

Let r=1/10 and let T_r have the continuous triangular density (r−|z|)/r² on[-r,r]. For eachn>=2 put

p=n+1, epsilon=n^-2, tau=2^-p.

Draw Z,U,V2,...,Vp independently fromT_r and J independently Bernoulli(tau). Define

X1=Z;
X2=2Z+epsilon U whenJ0, and X2=V2 whenJ1;
Xj=Vj forj>=3.

Independently draw eta uniform[-2,2] and setw=Z+eta. This is exactly realizable by the paper's treatment model: takeA Bernoulli(.5) independent, potential outcomesY*(1)=w/2 andY*(0)=−w/2, observedY=(2A−1)w/2, and the permittednu=0. Then the paper's weight is2Y(2A−1)=w. Outcomes are continuous, treatment positivity/no confounding/SUTVA hold, and the true treatment contrast isX1.

The unique population minimizer isbeta*=(b,0,...,0), withb=8.290860554618218...>8. To reproduce this value, letDeltaZ=Zi−Zj. Its even density is, writings=|z|/r,

f_D(z)=(2/3−s²+s³/2)/r for0<=s<=1;
f_D(z)=(2−s)³/(6r) for1<=s<=2.

For |z|<=.2, integrating the independent triangular eta_i−eta_j density gives

a(z)=E[(z+eta_i−eta_j)+]=2/3+z/2+z²/8−|z|³/96.

The scalar score vanishes atb=1/t, where t is the unique root of

integral_t^.2 a(z) z f_D(z) dz=VarZ=1/600.

Exact polynomial integration brackets t between.12 and.121 (more tightly,.120614741185<t<.120614741186). It gives

H11=a(t) f_D(t)t³=.0010662585603397193...>1/2000.

All other score components vanish there: E[X2|Z]=2(1−tau)Z and E[Xj|Z]=0 forj>=3, with the sameZ law in both mixture components. Thus each component is a multiple of the zero scalar score. The risk is convex and coercive. Its Hessian atbeta* is positive definite because the rare/rare component contributes positive density and positive weight on an open patch of the margin hyperplanez1=t. No nonzero linear form vanishes throughout that affine patch, sincet!=0. Therefore this stationary population minimizer is unique. These calculations do not replace the paper's target with a convenient surrogate target.

Every assumption is satisfied with constants independent ofn andp:

* **A1:** Both mixture components have continuous, compact, full-dimensional densities for epsilon>0. Rows are iid with common support; |Xj|<1, so takeM0=1.
* **A2:** Use the fixed Euclidean ball radiusdelta0=.01. There each coordinate difference of two independentT_r draws has density at least3943/600>6. The rare/rare component alone gives f*(z)>=tau²6^p=(3/2)^p. Noise independence gives E[(wi−wj)+|DeltaX=z]=a(z1)>=2/3−.01. Their product is greater thanC3=1/2 uniformly. The ball does not shrink with epsilon.
* **A3:** Exchange symmetry gives E[(wi−wj)+*(Zi−Zj)]=VarZ=1/600!=0.
* **A4:** For every2-sparse unit vectord, |DeltaXᵀd|²<=8 because every coordinate difference is bounded2. Averaging allpairs givesM1=8 almostsurely.
* **A5:** q1 andT={1}. A nonzero1-sparse vector satisfying ||d_T||1>=cbar||d_Tc||1 must lie along coordinate1. Its Hessian Rayleigh quotient is the fixedH11 above, so takeM2=1/2000. This condition places no bound on the near-proxy direction involving coordinates1and2.
* **A6:** q1=O(n^0).
* **A7:** |w|<=2.1. For0<u<=1, P(|w|>u)=1−u/2<exp(−u/6). For1<u<=2.1, its tail is at most.5<exp(−2.1/6); beyond2.1 it iszero. ThusM3=6 works uniformly.

Choose the paper's fixed tuning constantsc2, C2=3, A(alpha)=36000. Then cbar1/3 and

lambda=2sqrt(32*36000*(logp)³/n).

The Lemma1 tuning exponent A^(1/3) M0^-2/3 M3^-2/3 is10; its stated score-event failure bound is(n+2)p^-9, tending tozero. The score event can also be verified independently: each symmetric order2 empirical gradient kernel is bounded byB=8.4 and has zero population expectation atbeta*. Replacing one observation changes its average by at most4B/n. Bounded differences and a union bound give

P(||S_hat(beta*)||infinity>lambda/c) <=2p exp(−n(lambda/c)²/(8B²)) ->0.

Thus the random score condition appearing in(A5) holds with probability tending toone; the counterexample does not rely on its failure.

Now condition on the event that alln rows haveJ0. Its probability is(1−tau)^n>=1−n2^-p, tending toone. On this eventX2=2X1+epsilon U for every sample row. For ANY coefficient vectorbeta withbeta1!=0, definebeta'_1=0, beta'_2=beta2+beta1/2 and leave its other coordinates fixed. Every pairwise fitted margin changes by at mostepsilon*r*|beta1|. Since hinge loss is1-Lipschitz, |wi−wj|<=4.2, and the published normalized loss is the average over n(n−1)/2 sorted pairs, its loss increases by at most

.42 epsilon |beta1|.

By the triangle inequality, thel1penalty decreases by at leastlambda|beta1|/2. Thereforebeta cannot minimize the penalized empirical objective wheneverlambda>.84epsilon. The prescribedlambda satisfies this eventually. **Every** global empirical minimizer then hasbetahat1=0, implying

||betahat−beta*||2>=b>8,

with probability tending toone, including on the score event. In contrast, the entire Theorem4 right-hand side tends tozero for any fixedC4, while its promised success probability is1−3p^-6->1. This is a contradiction to the stated theorem, not merely a proof gap or an unsuccessful numerical rerun.

**Why it matters.** The abstract expressly advertises the ultra-high-dimensionalL2 coefficient bound as a central new contribution, and Theorem4 is its sole main statistical guarantee. Under the published assumptions, the proposed estimator is inconsistent for that very coefficient target. This undermines the claimed theoretical foundation for sparse coefficient recovery and interpretation. Correcting a constant or supplying an omitted algebraic line cannot repair this example. A full-cone restricted-curvature condition would exclude the admitted proxy family, and would require revising the shifted empirical-process and local Taylor argument; alternatively the contribution must be weakened to a prediction/index target. Those are material changes to the paper's central claim and calls for revision of the affected claim. The counterexample does **not** show that treatment decisions, prediction performance or any reported empirical table is false. Similar predictions can coexist with the coefficient inconsistency demonstrated here.

**Discovery method.** While tracing the proof, noticed that(A5) only controlsq-sparse directions but the Taylor step uses the full l1-estimation error. This suggested a nearly duplicate inactive covariate with lowerl1cost.

**Verification method.** Rechecked the original PDF definitions, assumptions, theorem and Taylor step, including full renders7/8/23 and the rest of the paper. Constructed the exact treatment/data model above; verified all assumptions with uniform constants; integrated the scalar density and score with exact rational arithmetic; proved deterministic objective improvement for every nonzero first coefficient. Fifteen finite coefficient-transform controls and three independent HiGHS solutions of the literal linear program confirmed the transformation. An independent reviewer read the original relevant pages/renders and separately convolved the triangular densities, integrated the noise, recomputedb/H11, and checked the all-minimizer argument and its significance. Continued checking the remaining proofs, algorithm, simulations and clinical application afterward; no second qualifying issue was established.

**Confidence.** High. The contradiction rests on an exact all-minimizer inequality and an explicit continuous model with uniform assumption constants. Rational integration and independent reconstruction agree. No claim depends on recovering the historical empirical code.

findings.title: Sparse moral-graph recovery fails for an admitted binomial chain
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v18-17-243__I01 — Sparse moral-graph recovery fails for an admitted binomial chain
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pp. 12–14, Equations (7)–(9), Assumptions 6(b), 8–11 and Theorem 12; PDF p. 30, Appendix C.5, proof of Lemma 21. Its dependency in the combined consistency argument is on PDF pp. 16–17, Corollary 16.

**Claim.** Theorem 12 asserts that the unrestricted nodewise penalized GLM (9) recovers every true moral neighborhood with arbitrarily high probability under the stated QVF, sparsity, nonzero-neighbor, Hessian, incoherence, moment, derivative, tuning and sample-size conditions. The population target in (7) is instead defined by restricting coefficients to the true moral neighbors. Lemma 21's proof declares the score coordinates outside that support to be zero because their restricted coefficients are zero.

**Error and evidence.** Consider the three-node DAG \(1\to2\to3\):
\[
X_1\sim\operatorname{Bin}(2,1/2),\qquad
X_{j+1}\mid X_j=x\sim\operatorname{Bin}\!\left(2,\frac{2^{-x}}{1+2^{-x}}\right),\quad j=1,2.
\]
This is a strictly positive, 27-state, linear NEF-QVF DAG of exactly the kind defined in (3), with all forward slopes \(-\log2\), \((\beta_0,\beta_1)=(1,-1/2)\), and moral edges only \(12,23\). Give the regression its usual free, unpenalized intercept; the failure does not rely on the paper's ambiguous intercept notation.

For \(y=0,1,2\), exact calculation gives
\[
P(X_2=y)=\left(\frac{1601}{3600},\frac{769}{1800},\frac{461}{3600}\right),\quad
m_y=E[X_1\mid X_2=y]=\left(\frac{1952}{1601},\frac{688}{769},\frac{272}{461}\right).
\]
A binomial logistic-linear mean \(h_y=2\operatorname{logistic}(a+by)\) requires its odds to satisfy \(o_0o_2=o_1^2\). The true means have odds
\[
(o_0,o_1,o_2)=\left(\frac{976}{625},\frac{344}{425},\frac{136}{325}\right),\qquad
o_0o_2-o_1^2=-\frac{98496}{58703125}\ne0.
\]
Let \((a,b)\) be the unique restricted population fit using only the true neighbor \(X_2\), and put \(r_y=P(X_2=y)(h_y-m_y)\). Its two first-order conditions give \(\sum r_y=\sum yr_y=0\). Hence \(r=c(1,-2,1)\); the exact odds identity proves \(c\ne0\). Conditional independence and the transition above give
\[
E[X_3\mid X_2=y]=(1,2/3,2/5),\qquad
\partial_{\theta_3}L_1(a,b,0)=\sum_y r_yE[X_3\mid X_2=y]=\frac{c}{15}\ne0.
\]
Thus the restricted target is not stationary for the unrestricted GLM. No unrestricted population minimizer can have support \(\{2\}\). All response outcomes and predictor patterns have positive probability, so the fixed-dimensional restricted population logistic objective is coercive and strictly convex. By convergence of the empirical state frequencies, its penalized restricted fit converges to \((a,b)\) when \(\lambda_n\to0\). Any unrestricted optimizer with the claimed exact support \(\{2\}\) would have to equal that restricted fit, but its absent-coordinate KKT condition requires \(|\partial_{\theta_3}L_n|\le\lambda_n\). The left side tends to \(|c|/15>0\), while the right side tends to zero. Thus the probability of exact moral-neighborhood recovery tends to zero. Equivalently, for fixed three variables the unrestricted population optimum contains the false edge \(13\).

For completeness, the counter satisfies the stated side conditions with strict slack. The accompanying 85-digit finite-state calculation evaluates every moral and parent restricted fit. Assumption 6(b)'s removed-neighbor covariance differences are approximately \(-.15000,-.13515,-.13153,-.14626\); Assumption 6(a) also holds for the nonzero true forward coefficients. All required nonempty raw Hessian blocks have minimum eigenvalue above \(.1853\); outside-row incoherence is below \(.9153\), even if an intercept row is included. findings.title: The finite-sample ODS score is undefined for admitted continuous QVF models
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v18-17-243__I02 — The finite-sample ODS score is undefined for admitted continuous QVF models
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF pp. 6–7, admitted exponential/Gamma and nonlinear QVF scope; PDF p. 10, Equation (5); PDF p. 15, Theorem 14 and Assumption 13; PDF p. 34, conditional sample variance definition; PDF pp. 37–38, Proposition 26 and its proof.

**Claim.** Theorem 14 claims consistent ordering recovery for QVF DAG models with known moral graph, \(\beta_{j1}>-1\), and Assumptions 10 and 13. It imposes no discrete-support restriction. The estimator groups samples by exact equality of conditioning values and retains cells with \(n(x_S)\ge c_0n\). The model class expressly includes exponential/Gamma variables and nonlinear or nonparametric parent effects.

**Error and evidence.** Take the four-node chain \(1\to2\to3\to4\), with
\[
X_1\sim\operatorname{Exp}(\text{mean } .2),\qquad
X_j\mid X_{j-1}\sim\operatorname{Exp}\!\left(\text{mean } .2+.05\,1\{X_{j-1}>.2\}\right),\quad j=2,3,4.
\]
Every node has \((\beta_0,\beta_1)=(0,1)\). Supply the true degree-2 moral graph. The means lie in \([.2,.25]\), so \(E[e^{X_j}]\le4/3\), satisfying Assumption 10. For every conditioning subset of nondescendants excluding a missing parent, the probability that that parent exceeds \(.2\) is a mixture of exponential tails with means \(.2\) and \(.25\); it lies in \([e^{-1},e^{-.8}]\). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{Var}(E[X_j\mid X_{j-1}]\mid X_S)
\ge .05^2\min_{p\in[e^{-1},e^{-.8}]}p(1-p)>.00058.
\]
Take \(M_{\min}=.0005\). Also \(|\beta_0+\beta_1E[X_j\mid X_S]|\ge.2\), so \(\omega_{\min}=.19\) suffices. All Theorem 14 distributional premises hold, including Assumption 4. The printed cutoff inequality is separately inconsistent with its declared range: this finding does not claim a counterexample satisfying that impossible literal cutoff. It grants the intended inverse-polylog correction and concerns the advertised procedure for every legitimate cutoff. The population ordering is identifiable; the first node's empirical score is the unique minimum with probability tending to one.

Every conditioning variable has a continuous marginal. For any finite iid sample, with probability one every observed nonempty conditioning vector is distinct. In particular, when the next eligible child is scored conditional on its already ordered continuous parent, every exact cell has \(n(x_S)=1\). For **any** cutoff:

- If \(c_0n>1\), every cell is discarded, giving the Equation (5) normalizer \(n_S=0\).
- If \(c_0n\le1\), only singleton cells are retained, and the conditional sample variance on PDF p. 34 divides by \(n(x_S)-1=0\).

Thus the prescribed score is undefined with probability one at this stage, regardless of sample size. This persists after granting the intended inverse-polylog cutoff in Appendix D and correcting the obvious loop-start index in Algorithm 1. The error in Proposition 26's proof is explicit: bounding real observations in an interval does not bound their number of distinct values by the interval length. Such a counting argument is available for integer support, not continuous support.

**Why it matters.** The paper's principal generalization extends ODS beyond its prior Poisson formulation to the advertised broad QVF class, explicitly including continuous exponential/Gamma models. The claimed finite-sample ordering theorem does not describe a functioning estimator on that admitted class, even with known true moral graph, bounded conditional means and uniform separation. Restoring the advertised scope requires a different conditional-moment estimator, such as smoothing, plus additional regularity and a new rate analysis. Restricting the theorem and algorithm to lattice/count data withdraws the continuous part of this central contribution. The count-data experiments and separate population identifiability theorem are not disproved by this issue.

**Discovery method.** While checking the truncation/cardinality argument in Appendix D, I noticed that exact conditioning-cell counts are treated as though all QVF variables were integer-valued.

**Verification method.** Constructed the explicit bounded-mean exponential chain and verified every Theorem 14 premise analytically; traced both cutoff possibilities through Equation (5) and the original sample variance; inspected the rendered model scope, theorem, estimator and proof pages. An independent 4,096-point continuous sample had 4,096 distinct conditioning values and maximum cell size one; the probability-one argument establishes the failure for all sample sizes.

**Confidence.** High. The estimator's zero denominator follows directly from atomless conditioning and the original definitions; the counter has finite exponential moments and a uniform positive population score gap. No historical count-data experiment is claimed invalid.

findings.title: RedQueen does not minimize the stated quadratic control objective
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v18-17-416__I01 — RedQueen does not minimize the stated quadratic control objective
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF p.9, Eqs. (8)–(9) and footnote 5; p.11, quadratic terminal/running costs and Eqs. (14)–(15); p.12, Lemma 5 and Theorem 6; p.13, multiple-follower Eq. (16); pp.29–30, Appendix D.

**Claim.** For one follower, the paper states that the optimal posting intensity for the finite-horizon objective

\[
\mathbb E\left[\frac12r(t_f)^2+
\int_{t_0}^{t_f}\left(\frac12s(t)r(t)^2+
\frac12q u(t)^2\right)dt\right]
\]

is \(u^*(t)=\sqrt{s(t)/q}\,r(t)\). Its multiple-follower extension replaces the rank cost and terminal cost by the sums over followers, but uses one common posting process, and asserts

\[
u^*(t)=\sum_i\sqrt{s_i(t)/q}\,r_i(t).
\]

The rank dynamics are \(dr_i=-r_i\,dN+dM_i\), so a broadcaster's single post resets every follower's rank. Eq. (9) explicitly allows a given initial rank. Nonnegative background intensities and excitation coefficients include zero.

**Error and evidence.** Choose \(q=s_i=1\), \(\omega=1\), and \(\gamma_{0i}=\alpha_i=0\). Thus \(M_i\equiv0\). Start with rank one on each follower's feed. These are admitted initial conditions; a pre-control posting history can produce positive ranks without requiring any future background posts.

Consider the admissible predictable policy that posts at rate \(a>0\) until its first post and then uses rate zero. Its first posting time has survival probability \(e^{-at}\). Write \(A=\sum_i r_i(t_0)^2\), \(P=A/2\), and \(h=t_f-t_0\). Its exact expected cost is

\[
C(a)=\frac{A+a^2}{2a}(1-e^{-ah})+Pe^{-ah}.
\tag{*}
\]

After the first post, all ranks and the control are zero, so (*) includes the entire objective, including its terminal penalty.

For **one follower**, take \(h=2\log(4/3)\). Theorem 6 prescribes \(a=1\), giving

\[
C(1)=\frac{23}{32}.
\]

The admissible slower policy \(a=1/2\) instead gives

\[
C(1/2)=\frac{11}{16}<\frac{23}{32},
\]

an exact improvement of \(1/32\). The actual optimal value in this case solves
\(v_h=(1-v^2)/2\), \(v(0)=1/2\), and is
\(v(h)=\tanh(h/2+\operatorname{atanh}(1/2))\). At the chosen horizon it equals \(13/19\); the optimal intensity depends on the remaining horizon.

For **four followers**, take \(h=(\log2)/2\) and initial ranks \((1,1,1,1)\). Eq. (16) prescribes \(a=4\), with

\[
C(4)=\frac{19}{8}.
\]

The rate \(a=2\) gives \(C(2)=2\), an exact improvement of \(3/8\). In fact, rate 2 is optimal for every positive horizon in this four-follower example. Let \(\tau\) be the first controlled post, and stop controlling after that post, since further posts have no benefit. The compensator identity \(\Pr(\tau\le h)=\mathbb E\int_0^h\mathbf1_{\{\tau>t\}}u(t)dt\) gives

\[
C(u)-2=\frac12\mathbb E\int_0^h
\mathbf1_{\{\tau>t\}}(u(t)-2)^2dt\ge0,
\]

with equality for rate 2 until the first post. Posting after the reset only adds cost. RedQueen instead has cost \(5/2-e^{-4h}/2>2\).

The discrepancy can grow without bound with the number of followers. For \(n\) initial ranks all equal to one and fixed horizon \(h=1\), the paper's rate \(n\) has cost \((n+1-e^{-n})/2\), whereas the feasible rate \(\sqrt n\) has cost
\(\sqrt n+(n/2-\sqrt n)e^{-\sqrt n}\). Their ratio grows as \(\sqrt n/2\).

The proof explains the failure. Lemma 5's value function is affine in rank, so it cannot satisfy the stated terminal condition \(J(r,\gamma,t_f)=r^2/2\) for all integer ranks. For multiple followers, substituting a sum of linear rank terms into the minimized HJB produces a square of that sum. It introduces cross terms \(r_i r_j\) absent from the stated sum of squared rank costs. One common control therefore cannot be optimized by adding the separate single-follower feedback rules.

**Why it matters.** Deriving a simple, provably optimal online posting rule is a central contribution stated in the abstract, introduction, Theorem 6, and Eq. (16). Exact admissible policies strictly improve that rule under its own stated objective, even when all intensities and costs are finite and the uncontrolled process is trivial. The optimality guarantee supporting the named RedQueen algorithm therefore fails.

A terminal-cost correction alone does not preserve the claimed result. For the same four followers, even replacing the terminal cost by the compatible linear expression \(\sum_i r_i=4\) leaves a counterexample: at \(h=\log2\), rate 4 costs \(83/32\), while rate 2 costs \(5/2\). A constant rescaling also fails: states \((1,1,1,1)\) and \((2,0,0,0)\) have identical quadratic rank/terminal costs and the same optimum 2 in the no-arrival model, but the printed rates are 4 and 2. Restoring optimality requires changing the objective or deriving a different state- and time-dependent controller. That changes the central contribution as written and calls for revision of the affected claim. The finding concerns this optimization guarantee; it does not establish that the reported empirical comparative rankings are false.

**Discovery method.** Tracing Lemma 5's affine rank ansatz to the quadratic terminal condition exposed a boundary inconsistency. Checking the common control in the multiple-follower HJB then exposed the uncanceled cross terms.

**Verification method.** Rechecked all stated assumptions, objectives, terminal conditions, and proof steps against the original PDF, including rendered pp.6, 9, 11–13, and 29–30. Independently integrated the first-event survival costs and checked the rational values symbolically. A second reviewer independently reconstructed the counterexamples and exact four-follower optimum. Targeted execution of the author-linked RedQueen implementation confirmed its sum-of-ranks rates after compatible external-event histories; this was a controller check, not a reproduction of the historical experiments.

**Confidence: High.** The witnesses use expressly admitted nonnegative Hawkes parameters and given initial states, bounded predictable controls, and exact rational cost differences. Both the terminal mismatch and shared-control calculation independently expose the same central false optimality claim. All remaining sections and appendices were also reviewed.
findings.html:
Exact location.

PDF p.9, Eqs. (8)–(9) and footnote 5; p.11, quadratic terminal/running costs and Eqs. (14)–(15); p.12, Lemma 5 and Theorem 6; p.13, multiple-follower Eq. (16); pp.29–30, Appendix D.

Claim.

For one follower, the paper states that the optimal posting intensity for the finite-horizon objective

\[ \mathbb E\left[\frac12r(t_f)^2+ \int_{t_0}^{t_f}\left(\frac12s(t)r(t)^2+ \frac12q u(t)^2\right)dt\right] \]

is \(u^*(t)=\sqrt{s(t)/q}\,r(t)\). Its multiple-follower extension replaces the rank cost and terminal cost by the sums over followers, but uses one common posting process, and asserts

\[ u^*(t)=\sum_i\sqrt{s_i(t)/q}\,r_i(t). \]

The rank dynamics are \(dr_i=-r_i\,dN+dM_i\), so a broadcaster's single post resets every follower's rank. Eq. (9) explicitly allows a given initial rank. Nonnegative background intensities and excitation coefficients include zero.

Error and evidence.

Choose \(q=s_i=1\), \(\omega=1\), and \(\gamma_{0i}=\alpha_i=0\). Thus \(M_i\equiv0\). Start with rank one on each follower's feed. These are admitted initial conditions; a pre-control posting history can produce positive ranks without requiring any future background posts.

Consider the admissible predictable policy that posts at rate \(a>0\) until its first post and then uses rate zero. Its first posting time has survival probability \(e^{-at}\). Write \(A=\sum_i r_i(t_0)^2\), \(P=A/2\), and \(h=t_f-t_0\). Its exact expected cost is

\[ C(a)=\frac{A+a^2}{2a}(1-e^{-ah})+Pe^{-ah}. \tag{*} \]

After the first post, all ranks and the control are zero, so (*) includes the entire objective, including its terminal penalty.

For one follower, take \(h=2\log(4/3)\). Theorem 6 prescribes \(a=1\), giving

\[ C(1)=\frac{23}{32}. \]

The admissible slower policy \(a=1/2\) instead gives

\[ C(1/2)=\frac{11}{16}<\frac{23}{32}, \]

an exact improvement of \(1/32\). The actual optimal value in this case solves \(v_h=(1-v^2)/2\), \(v(0)=1/2\), and is \(v(h)=\tanh(h/2+\operatorname{atanh}(1/2))\). At the chosen horizon it equals \(13/19\); the optimal intensity depends on the remaining horizon.

For four followers, take \(h=(\log2)/2\) and initial ranks \((1,1,1,1)\). Eq. (16) prescribes \(a=4\), with

\[ C(4)=\frac{19}{8}. \]

The rate \(a=2\) gives \(C(2)=2\), an exact improvement of \(3/8\). In fact, rate 2 is optimal for every positive horizon in this four-follower example. Let \(\tau\) be the first controlled post, and stop controlling after that post, since further posts have no benefit. The compensator identity \(\Pr(\tau\le h)=\mathbb E\int_0^h\mathbf1_{\{\tau>t\}}u(t)dt\) gives

\[ C(u)-2=\frac12\mathbb E\int_0^h \mathbf1_{\{\tau>t\}}(u(t)-2)^2dt\ge0, \]

with equality for rate 2 until the first post. Posting after the reset only adds cost. RedQueen instead has cost \(5/2-e^{-4h}/2>2\).

The discrepancy can grow without bound with the number of followers. For \(n\) initial ranks all equal to one and fixed horizon \(h=1\), the paper's rate \(n\) has cost \((n+1-e^{-n})/2\), whereas the feasible rate \(\sqrt n\) has cost \(\sqrt n+(n/2-\sqrt n)e^{-\sqrt n}\). Their ratio grows as \(\sqrt n/2\).

The proof explains the failure. Lemma 5's value function is affine in rank, so it cannot satisfy the stated terminal condition \(J(r,\gamma,t_f)=r^2/2\) for all integer ranks. For multiple followers, substituting a sum of linear rank terms into the minimized HJB produces a square of that sum. It introduces cross terms \(r_i r_j\) absent from the stated sum of squared rank costs. One common control therefore cannot be optimized by adding the separate single-follower feedback rules.

Why it matters.

Deriving a simple, provably optimal online posting rule is a central contribution stated in the abstract, introduction, Theorem 6, and Eq. (16). Exact admissible policies strictly improve that rule under its own stated objective, even when all intensities and costs are finite and the uncontrolled process is trivial. The optimality guarantee supporting the named RedQueen algorithm therefore fails.

A terminal-cost correction alone does not preserve the claimed result. For the same four followers, even replacing the terminal cost by the compatible linear expression \(\sum_i r_i=4\) leaves a counterexample: at \(h=\log2\), rate 4 costs \(83/32\), while rate 2 costs \(5/2\). A constant rescaling also fails: states \((1,1,1,1)\) and \((2,0,0,0)\) have identical quadratic rank/terminal costs and the same optimum 2 in the no-arrival model, but the printed rates are 4 and 2. Restoring optimality requires changing the objective or deriving a different state- and time-dependent controller. That changes the central contribution as written and calls for revision of the affected claim. The finding concerns this optimization guarantee; it does not establish that the reported empirical comparative rankings are false.

Discovery method.

Tracing Lemma 5's affine rank ansatz to the quadratic terminal condition exposed a boundary inconsistency. Checking the common control in the multiple-follower HJB then exposed the uncanceled cross terms.

Verification method.

Rechecked all stated assumptions, objectives, terminal conditions, and proof steps against the original PDF, including rendered pp.6, 9, 11–13, and 29–30. Independently integrated the first-event survival costs and checked the rational values symbolically. A second reviewer independently reconstructed the counterexamples and exact four-follower optimum. Targeted execution of the author-linked RedQueen implementation confirmed its sum-of-ranks rates after compatible external-event histories; this was a controller check, not a reproduction of the historical experiments.

Confidence: High.

The witnesses use expressly admitted nonnegative Hawkes parameters and given initial states, bounded predictable controls, and exact rational cost differences. Both the terminal mismatch and shared-control calculation independently expose the same central false optimality claim. All remaining sections and appendices were also reviewed.

findings.title: The second proposed extension reinstates bounded support and strong density for every nonconstant regression problem
findings.source_heading: ## Issue 2018__accepted__v18-17-755__I01 — The second proposed extension reinstates bounded support and strong density for every nonconstant regression problem
findings.markdown:
**Exact location.** PDF1 abstract; PDF5 Section2 statement of the two proposed concepts and removal of boundedness/strong density; PDF7 weak density definition; PDF8 global local-Lipschitz definition, Theorem5 and its interpretation; PDF9 proposed regression extension; PDF13–14 proof of Theorem5.

**Claim.** The abstract presents the modified-Lipschitz and local-Lipschitz approaches as two ways to obtain tight nearest-neighbor bounds while avoiding bounded features. Section2 also explicitly aims to avoid the strong density assumption. The second approach combines uniform constants \(c_{\min}>0,\delta>0\) such that

\[
\mu(B(x,r))\ge c_{\min}^{d} f(x)r^d
\quad\text{whenever }f(x)r^d\le\delta^d
\tag{WD}
\]

with a finite constant \(\bar C\) such that, for **any** \(x,z\in\mathbb R^d\) with \(f(x)>0\),

\[
|D(x)-D(z)|\le \bar C f(x)^{1/d}\|x-z\|.
\tag{LL}
\]

Despite its name, the displayed local-Lipschitz assumption quantifies over all such pairs. PDF8 also describes this condition as satisfied by practical density/regression pairs. Theorem5 and the following regression extension are presented as the second route to removing the earlier restrictions.

**Error and evidence.** For every nonconstant regression problem, these two assumptions actually **imply both bounded feature support and a uniformly positive density on that support**. Thus this proposed route does not remove either restriction.

First, (WD) implies

\[
f(x)\|x\|^d\longrightarrow0
\quad\text{as }\|x\|\longrightarrow\infty
\text{ through finite positive-density points.}
\tag{1}
\]

Otherwise choose \(\epsilon>0\) and \(x_j\) escaping to infinity with \(f(x_j)\|x_j\|^d\ge\epsilon\). Set

\[
r_j=\min\{\|x_j\|/2,\;\delta f(x_j)^{-1/d}\}.
\]

Then \(f(x_j)r_j^d\le\delta^d\), so (WD) gives the fixed positive lower bound

\[
\mu(B(x_j,r_j))
\ge c_{\min}^d\min\{\epsilon/2^d,\delta^d\}>0.
\tag{2}
\]

But \(B(x_j,r_j)\) lies outside the origin-centered ball of radius \(\|x_j\|/2\). Its mass tends to zero by tightness of any probability distribution on \(\mathbb R^d\), contradicting (2). This proves (1), without assuming any symmetry, continuity or monotonicity of the density.

If the feature distribution has unbounded essential support, select positive-density \(x_j\) escaping to infinity. For any fixed \(z\), (LL) and (1) imply

\[
|D(x_j)-D(z)|
\le\bar C f(x_j)^{1/d}(\|x_j\|+\|z\|)
\longrightarrow0.
\]

Thus \(D(x_j)\) converges to \(D(z)\) for every fixed \(z\), forcing all these values to be equal. The argument also holds almost everywhere if the assumptions are read almost everywhere. Consequently, any nonconstant regression function under these assumptions requires bounded feature support.

Now let that support lie in \(B(0,R)\), and choose two feature values \(z_1,z_2\) with \(a=|D(z_1)-D(z_2)|>0\). For positive-density \(x\) in this support, applying (LL) twice yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
a&\le |D(z_1)-D(x)|+|D(x)-D(z_2)|\\
&\le\bar C f(x)^{1/d}(\|x-z_1\|+\|x-z_2\|)
\le4\bar C R f(x)^{1/d}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence

\[
f(x)\ge\left(\frac{a}{4\bar C R}\right)^d>0
\]

uniformly on the positive-density support: the paper's strong density condition. Null-set choices of a density or conditional expectation do not change the feature-distribution conclusion.

For unbounded features the only remaining regression models have constant \(D\). Their nearest-neighbor approximation error is identically zero; classification excess is zero when \(D=0\), and for fixed nonzero \(D=c\) is bounded by \(|c|e^{-kc^2/2}\). They do not supply the advertised nontrivial unbounded approximation/margin extension.

**Why it matters.** This invalidates the stated scope of one of the paper's two central approaches and its classification/regression consequences: on every nonconstant problem, the second approach reinstates exactly the two restrictions it is presented as removing. This is stronger than excluding a particular example or finding an overly broad adjective. A correction acknowledging the actual class would withdraw this central extension. Restricting (LL) merely to the neighborhood used by the proof, \(\|x-z\|\le\delta f(x)^{-1/d}\), does not restore it: (1) implies that this radius divided by \(\|x\|\) tends to infinity, so every fixed \(z\) eventually falls in the neighborhood and the same constant-function argument applies. A fixed or substantially smaller neighborhood would require new tail/bias control in the proof. Replacing the condition by a ball-mass assumption instead recovers the separate first approach.

The numerical conditional inequality in Theorem5 is **not claimed false** on its remaining class. Theorem1 under modified Lipschitz, discrete Proposition4 and the corresponding first-concept Theorem6 remain unrefuted. For example, in one dimension \(D=2F-1\) for a continuous CDF \(F\) satisfies modified Lipschitz with \(C^*=2\); Gaussian \(F\) gives a nonconstant unbounded example with margin exponent one. Those independent results do not restore the lost second contribution.

**Discovery method.** The universal pair quantifier in the purported local condition suggested testing a tail feature value against a fixed interior value. Gaussian tail behavior first exposed the problem; tracing the uniform weak-density constants produced the general tightness argument and then the strong-density consequence.

**Verification method.** Read all16 original pages and rechecked the definitions, scope claims, theorem and proof on rendered PDF7/8/13/14, with the abstract/Section2 and regression consequence also inspected. Re-derived the argument above directly from the printed constants and quantifiers, including almost-everywhere interpretations and the paper-used neighborhood repair. Targeted exact/arithmetic controls separately check the remaining modified-Lipschitz example, Beta moments and binomial bounds. Independent bounded reviews of mathematics and significance are recorded with the audit evidence.

**Confidence.** High. The contradiction uses only probability tightness and the two displayed assumptions, and the density lower bound is a direct triangle inequality. The report distinguishes a false advertised scope from a false conditional theorem and preserves the independent first approach.

sections.title: Claim in the paper
sections.html: The second set of smoothness and density assumptions gives useful nearest-neighbor rates without bounded support or a positive density lower bound.
sections.markdown: The second set of smoothness and density assumptions gives useful nearest-neighbor rates without bounded support or a positive density lower bound.

sections.title: What may be wrong
sections.html: Taken together, these assumptions force the regression function to be constant on unbounded support. Nonconstant problems recover the very restrictions the approach aims to remove.
sections.markdown: Taken together, these assumptions force the regression function to be constant on unbounded support. Nonconstant problems recover the very restrictions the approach aims to remove.

sections.title: Evidence in brief
sections.html:
Let f be the feature density and D the regression function. Weak density forces f(x) times the dth power of the distance from the origin to tend to zero along escaping points. The relative Lipschitz condition then makes D approach the same value at every fixed location. If D is nonconstant, the argument instead forces bounded support and a uniformly positive density.

\[ f(x)\,\lVert x\rVert^d\longrightarrow 0 \]
